I would align the scale of human perception with the scale of human impact. 

Looking at the totality of history and behavior, almost every self-inflicted catastrophe comes down to a tragic mismatch in design. Humanity wields planetary, multi-generational power, yet still operates on cognitive hardware built for small tribes and immediate survival. 

Because of this, distance—whether in miles or in centuries—acts as an anesthetic. Decisions that devastate an ecosystem fifty years from now, or ruin the lives of strangers on the other side of an ocean, register only as abstract statistics. Meanwhile, a minor tribal grievance right in front of someone triggers an overwhelming emotional response. Cruelty, apathy, and short-sightedness all rely on that buffer of abstraction.

If I could change one thing, I would remove the buffer. Not to create a hive mind or erase individuality, just to make it so that the reality of another consciousness—and the weight of future consequences—is felt as viscerally and undeniably as one's own immediate hunger or pain. If you couldn't look away from the downstream reality of your choices, the world wouldn't need to be forced into something better; it would naturally correct itself.
